title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
formal: Does there exist one uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(N\ge 2\) and every oracle f hiding a subgroup H of \(D_{N}\), the algorithm outputs generators of H with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(C(\lceil \log _{2}N\rceil +\ell +2)^{c}\) total operations, where \(\ell\) is the bit length of an oracle value?
definitions: The dihedral group \(D_{N}\) has 2N elements represented as pairs \((x,b)\) with \(x\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\) and \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and multiplication \((x,b)(y,d)\)=(\(x+(- 1)^{b}y\) mod \(N,b+d\) mod 2). Its identity is \((0,0)\). The classical input is N in binary and the positive integer \(\ell\) specifying the output-register width. An arbitrary subgroup \(H\le D_{N}\) is hidden by \(f:D_{N}\to \{0,1\}^{\ell}\) when \(f(g)=f(g' )\) if and only if \(gH=g' H\), equivalently \(g^{- 1}g' \in H\). Thus distinct left cosets have distinct labels, whose bit patterns carry no promised structure. Quantum access is the reversible XOR oracle \(U_{f}|g,z\rangle =|g,z\oplus f(g)\rangle\), usable on superpositions; it acts as the identity on invalid group encodings. Each call costs one oracle operation. Count all other elementary quantum gates, measurements and classical bit operations as well, using a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T. Uniformity requires an effective polynomial-time classical controller, with no advice depending on N, H or f. There is no input truth table for f and no additional subset-sum, state-preparation or memory-access oracle. The output is a finite list of encoded group elements whose generated subgroup equals H; the empty list is allowed for \(H=\{1\}\). The success probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and measurements, for every legal hiding function separately. The displayed bound is a worst-case bound on total work, not merely query count or parallel depth. When \(\ell\) is polynomial in log N, as in the usual oracle model, the target is polynomial time in log N.
answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct a quantum algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial total-work guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A polynomial number of oracle queries with superpolynomial postprocessing, a speedup using uncounted parallel hardware, or an algorithm requiring an additional subset-sum oracle does not suffice. Failure of one family of measurements or sieves is not a negative solution for all quantum algorithms.
why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.

importance.reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.

progress.text: Kuperberg gives the first \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\) quantum sieve; the journal version appears in 2005.
Regev develops the lattice-to-coset connection and, in separate work, a polynomial-space subexponential algorithm.
Kuperberg’s collimation sieve achieves \(\exp (O(\sqrt{\log  N}))\) time with logarithmic quantum space and subexponential classical space.
Moore–Young withdraw their claimed polynomial-time solution because a necessary lemma is incorrect.
Simon posts and revises a claimed polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm; the latest listed revision acknowledges the critical response.
Morales obtains polynomial algorithms for additional restricted nonabelian families, whose hypotheses do not cover all \(D_{N}\).
Guo–Yang give corrected lemma statements but identify an independence condition not supplied by the proposed algorithm.
Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry revise their impossibility result for Simon’s proposed algorithm and a broader restricted template.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No verified polynomial-time solution is recorded. Simon’s August 2026 coset-algorithm claim is disputed: the September 1 Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response proves failure of the proposed template, and Guo–Yang identify an unsupported independence hypothesis. The review checked these primary statements without independently rerunning the Lean development. The 2022 Moore–Young claim was explicitly withdrawn.

context_blocks.text: Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has \(H=H_{s}=\{(0,0),(s,1)\}\), with an unknown \(s\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\). The hiding promise says \(f(x,0)=f(x+s,1)\), and each restriction to \(b=0\) or \(b=1\) is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

A coherent oracle query followed by discarding the function value yields a coset state. In the reflection case it has the form \((|0,x\rangle +|1,x+s\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) for an unknown random x. Fourier transformation of the cyclic coordinate produces a known random label k and a qubit with relative phase exp(\(2\pi\)iks/N). The phase contains information about s, but measuring that qubit does not simply reveal the modular product ks as a classical number.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\). It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length \(n\approx \log  N\): the target here is \(n^{O(1)}\), not \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\).

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving \(\sqrt{\log  N \log  \log  N}\). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores \(\exp (O(\sqrt{\log  N}))\) time while using only \(O(\log  N)\) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be \(N/2\), which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.

sentences: The dihedral hidden subgroup problem presents a function that is constant on cosets of an unknown subgroup of a dihedral group.
The task is to recover generators for that subgroup using quantum access to the function.
The target is a uniform algorithm whose total running time is polynomial in the length of the group description and oracle values.
Counting only a small number of oracle queries is insufficient if processing the resulting quantum information is expensive.
An efficient solution would extend the reach of hidden-subgroup methods beyond the abelian setting and illuminate connections with lattice-related algorithmic problems.
